content_voiceover: This slide lays out the fifth edition of the WHO classification of AML, and it's worth knowing cold for boards. The big conceptual shift is on the left column: AML with defining genetic abnormalities. For most of these entities, you no longer need to hit the twenty percent blast threshold, the genetics alone are diagnostic. The classic ones are still here, APL with PML-RARA, core binding factor AML with RUNX1-RUNX1T1 or CBFB-MYH11, and AML with NPM1 mutation. But note the exceptions marked with an asterisk, BCR-ABL1 fusion, CEBPA mutation, and myelodysplasia-related AML still require that twenty percent blast cutoff, because those categories overlap biologically with other diseases like CML or MDS. On the right side is the older, morphology-based approach, AML defined by differentiation, which still requires blasts of twenty percent or more, things like AML without maturation or acute monocytic leukemia. The takeaway for exams is simple, genetics trumps morphology whenever a defining mutation or fusion is present.
keypoints: Genetic-defined AML usually skips the twenty percent blast requirement
Exceptions needing twenty percent blasts, BCR-ABL1, CEBPA, MDS-related AML
Core binding factor and APL fusions remain classic defining lesions
Differentiation-based AML categories still need twenty percent blasts
New entities added, KMT2A, MECOM, and NUP98 rearrangements
keypoint_voiceover: Remember, genetic abnormalities generally bypass the blast percentage rule, except for BCR-ABL1, CEBPA mutated, and myelodysplasia-related AML, which still need twenty percent blasts. The right column, defined by differentiation, is the traditional morphologic classification and always requires twenty percent blasts.
